pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 the modelling situations become scaling, area/perimeter, unit conversion and percentage — and crucially the child now selects among competing representations rather than being handed one. The practice is still the full cycle, but the interpret-back carries real-world stakes: a sale price must come back as pounds and pence a shopper would actually pay, a carpet answer must be an area that a room could hold. The teaching emphasis is (1) choosing a representation that fits the structure (a percentage bar for a discount, a scale diagram for a room, a double number line for a rate) and (2) explaining the final quantity in its own units and checking it is plausible.
bestPractices: Make representation CHOICE explicit: give one situation and ask which model (bar, scale diagram, double number line, table) exposes its structure, and why — the practice at this age is selecting, not just using
Route every percentage answer back to money: '£40 with 25% off is £30 — the £30 is what you actually pay', never leaving a bare 30 or 0.75
For area/perimeter, keep the two quantities distinct and interpret each in its own unit (cm² of carpet vs cm of edging) so the child does not blur area with length
Insist on a reasonableness check tied to the context: a sale price must be less than the original; a scaled recipe more than the original; a converted length the same physical size
Use numberless framing for multi-structure problems so the child models the situation before deciding which numbers to combine
keyRepresentations: Percentage bar model (100% strip partitioned for discount/increase)
Scale diagram / scaled drawing for area and length
Double number line and ratio table for scaling and rates
Area/perimeter rectangle with l, w labelled and formula alongside
commonMisconceptions: Gives the discount amount (£10 off) when asked the sale price (£30), or leaves the answer as a decimal (0.75) never returned to pounds
Confuses area and perimeter — adds sides when the situation needs area, or reports the carpet answer in cm instead of cm²
Applies a percentage as a raw number ('25% is 25') rather than a proportion of the specific amount
Picks a representation by habit rather than fit, so a rate problem gets a single bar that hides the two varying quantities
Scales additively (adds the same amount) instead of multiplicatively when enlarging a recipe or shape

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, real-world maths modelling means running the full cycle — choose a representation that fits the situation's structure, build it, compute, then interpret the result back in the right units with a plausibility check. At this age the new skill is SELECTING among competing models (percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line/ratio table, area rectangle) rather than being handed one. The recurring failure is answering with a by-product of the calculation (the discount £10, or the proportion 0.75) rather than the quantity the situation actually asked for (the £30 a shopper pays), and never sense-checking (a sale price must be below the original).

activities.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench
feedback: If a learner names £10 as the price: draw the percentage bar and shade discount vs part-left — 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Ask 'what does the shopper actually hand over?'

If a learner leaves 0.75 or 75 as the answer: ask '0.75 of WHAT?' and require conversion to £30 stated as money — a percentage answer ends in the unit of the quantity it is a percentage of, which here is pounds

If a learner subtracts 25 ('25% off means take 25') to get £15: anchor the percentage to the bar of £40 — 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10 — and contrast 25% of £40 (=£10) with 25% of £80 (=£20) to show it depends on the amount

If a learner reports the carpet answer in a length unit (cm or m) or adds the sides for an area question: keep area and length physically distinct — coverage of the floor is a squared unit (m² or cm²), the edge measured is a length (m or cm) — and do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity, with the squared area unit matching the length unit used (a room measured in metres gives m², so 4 m × 3 m = 12 m²)
activities.rationale: Modelling explicitly includes interpreting results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; a part-whole/percentage bar exposes proportional structure so a child can find and explain a sale price rather than manipulating numbers by rule. Building the situation model before computing, and making representation choice explicit, targets the age-appropriate skill of selecting rather than just using a model.
sourceClaims: Modelling includes interpreting mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflecting on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model
A percentage/part-whole bar exposes proportional structure so children can find a sale price and explain it, rather than manipulating numbers by rule
Keyword strategies backfire and children suspend sense-making; problem-specific supports and building the situation model before computing help children choose the right operation
learnerActions: Take a situation such as 'a £40 jacket has 25% off — what does a shopper pay?' and first choose which representation exposes its structure from a palette: percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line, or ratio table
Build a percentage bar: partition the 100% strip into quarters, shade off one quarter (the discount), and read what remains
State explicitly what each number refers to: £10 is the discount (25% of £40), 0.75 is the proportion of the original price remaining, and £30 is the price paid
Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)
Notice which representation you reach for — if you grab a single bar for a rate problem that has two varying quantities, ask whether it hides structure
activities.intendedInsight: When the question asks what the shopper pays, the answer is the part that STAYS (£30), not the part taken off (£10) nor the bare proportion (0.75); and a model is chosen to fit a situation's structure, with every answer returned to its real units and sense-checked.

activities.title: Defend the answer to a customer or tradesperson
feedback: Reject a bare '10' or '0.75' and ask the learner to say what each number refers to before accepting any answer
If the learner cannot justify plausibility, prompt: 'is the price you pay bigger or smaller than £40, and why must that always be true for a sale?'
activities.rationale: Articulating the interpret-back in words can help the learner attach each number to its referent and defend reasonableness — the discriminating skill, since both wrong answers are genuine by-products of a correct calculation. This is a complementary spoken route to the build task, not a required or superior replacement for it.
sourceClaims: Modelling includes interpreting mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflecting on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model
learnerActions: Work in role with a customer or decorator who only accepts an answer once it is stated as the real quantity they need
Answer the shopkeeper's probe 'you said 30 — is that the discount or what I pay?' by distinguishing the two
Answer the decorator's probe 'is that enough for a 4 m by 3 m room?' by stating an area with its unit (12 m²) and checking it is plausible
Voice the reasonableness check aloud: '£30 — less than £40, so for a sale it makes sense'
activities.intendedInsight: The reflective close of the modelling cycle can be spoken: you name which number is the discount, which is the proportion, and which is the quantity asked for, and you justify that it is sensible.

activities.title: Feel area as coverage, length as edge (optional spatial scaffold)
feedback: If a learner gives a length where an area is needed, or drops the squared unit, return to the physical distinction: coverage fills the floor (a squared unit), the edge runs around it (a length unit), and the squared unit must match the length unit used
activities.rationale: A room may make area-versus-perimeter felt for learners who confuse them, but the core structures at this age (percentage, rate, scale) are planar or numeric, so this remains subordinate to the 2D modelling work and should not displace it. Its benefit for most learners is untested; offer it where the area/length confusion is observed.
learnerActions: Cover the floor of a room to feel area as coverage, reported in a squared unit matching the measurements (e.g. m² of carpet needed for a metre-dimensioned room)
Measure around the edge of the same floor to feel length, reported as a length matching the measurements (e.g. m of skirting or edging)
Say out loud which quantity a given question asks for before computing, and match the unit to it
activities.intendedInsight: Area (coverage) and perimeter (edge length) are physically different quantities with different units; blurring them is the error, not a detail.

constraints: The modelling cycle is the objective: choosing a representation, computing, AND interpreting back with a reasonableness check. A scored step that accepts a bare correct number cannot force or observe the representation-choice and interpret-back, so use such checks only for isolated sub-skills (e.g. percentage of an amount) that feed the real modelling task.

A static labelled percentage bar or scale diagram can prime or remind what a representation shows, but on its own does not let the learner choose, compute, or interpret back; treat it as a reference card, not the teaching vehicle for the practice.

Keep area and length as distinct quantities with distinct units throughout; the area uses a squared unit (m² or cm²) that matches the length unit of the measurements and must not be reported as a length.

Every percentage answer must return to the real quantity the situation asks for, stated with its unit (e.g. the £30 a shopper actually pays when the question asks for the price paid) — never leave a bare 30, 75, or 0.75.
Enlarging a recipe or shape is multiplicative (scale by a factor), not additive (add the same amount); watch for additive scaling.
The room/coverage activity is an optional scaffold for learners who confuse area and perimeter, not a required step for every learner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are reproduced exactly from the row and cited only where they support a stated teaching principle; a citation does not establish that any specific activity here was tested for efficacy.

The original framed the 3D room as 'overkill' and the quiz/static image as unable to 'host the modelling cycle'. These are retained as scoped affordance/limit statements (recognition-only checks do not elicit representation-choice or interpret-back) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach.

The original row stated the room-carpet answer in cm² while giving the room as '4 m by 3 m'. This is an inherited unit inconsistency: 4×3=12 m², and only 120000 in cm². It was corrected so the squared area unit matches the length unit of the measurements (m² for a metre-dimensioned room). The original cm² wording is noted here, not offered to learners as correct.

Self-audit on the worked example: £40 with 25% off gives discount £10 (a quarter of £40), price paid £30, proportion remaining 0.75 — all internally consistent. 25% of £80 would be £20, confirming the percentage depends on the amount. No arithmetic errors found beyond the area-unit inconsistency corrected above, which is now resolved at every occurrence.

probeDeeper: Is the price you pay bigger or smaller than £40? Why must that be true for any sale?
If the discount were 25% of an £80 jacket instead, would the '£10' still be right? What changes?
Someone converts the sale price and writes £3000 — how would you know instantly that's wrong?
Show me on a bar which part is the discount and which part is what you pay — how do the two parts relate to the whole?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child distinguishing that '10' is the discount (25% of £40) and '0.75' is the fraction/proportion remaining, and that the price PAID is £30; and for a reasonableness check ('£30 is less than £40, which must be true for a sale'). A child who cannot say what 10 and 0.75 each refer to, or who names one of them as the price, is computing without modelling.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the discount as the sale price ('it's £10') — computes the change but not the resulting quantity the question asked for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the percentage bar and shade the discount vs the part left: 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Route the answer back through 'what does the shopper hand over?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names 10 as the price to pay and is untroubled that a £40 jacket now costs £10

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as a bare decimal or proportion ('0.75') and never converts it back into pounds and pence in the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the return trip: 0.75 of WHAT? Convert to £30 and state it as money. Practise ending every percentage problem in the currency it lives in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child offers 0.75 (or 75) as the answer with no unit and no sense that a shopper pays in £

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the percentage as a raw number ('25% off means take away 25') rather than a proportion of the specific £40
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the percentage to the bar of £40: 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10. Contrast 25% of £40 with 25% of £80 to show it depends on the amount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts 25 to get £15, ignoring that 25% must be taken OF the amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which quantity is asked when a situation mixes area and length — reports a carpet answer in cm instead of cm² (or adds sides for an area question)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep area and length as physically different things: cover the floor to feel cm² (coverage) vs measure the edge for cm (length). Do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the carpet/room follow-up the child gives a length where an area is needed, or omits the squared unit

responseLevels.gap: Names the discount (£10) or the proportion (0.75) as the final price, or gives a bare number with no unit; cannot say what each number refers to and does not check plausibility.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, distinguishes discount, proportion-left and price-paid, states £30 with its unit, checks it is below £40 as a sale must be, would reject an out-of-scale result, and transfers the choose-model→interpret→check habit to a fresh scaling, area or rate problem.
responseLevels.partial: Can, when prompted, identify that 10 is the discount and £30 is the price, and states the unit, but does not spontaneously sense-check (that a sale price must be below the original) and needs support to choose the fitting representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A £40 jacket has 25% off. A shopper says the answer is 10. Another says it's 0.75. What has each of them worked out, and what is the price the shopper actually pays? How would you know your final answer is sensible?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two wrong answers are both real by-products of a correct calculation, so arithmetic skill is not the tell — the discriminator is whether the child can attach each number to its referent in the situation and identify which one is the quantity the problem actually asked for, then sense-check it. Only genuine modelling separates 'the discount', 'the proportion left', and 'the price paid'.
